ACCESS AND AFFORDABILITY The University has developed a comprehensive enrollment management approach to foster access and affordability while also enhancing selectivity, quality, and student success.
These efforts include, but are not limited to, expansive recruitment strategies, predictive modeling, and an investment in financial aid.
These efforts have resulted in record applications and strong enrollments over the past 10 years.
URI was also able to avoid a loss in students during COVID as many schools experienced.
Student diversity, selectivity and quality have all improved each year.
Because of the University’s mission, the admissions policy is "selective" in that only students deemed prepared for university -level study are granted regular admission.

Due to Rhode Island’s size and declining number of high school graduates, the University enrolls a significant number of students from outside of Rhode Island.
Feedback from families that choose URI is that the University offers quality programs in a safe location at a good cost and value.
As part of the drive for accessibility and affordability, and recognizing the increasing educational diversity of potential students, the University maintains several programs for special populations and has starte d several new initiatives as well.
The University has worked to keep its tuition and fee rates affordable and competitive.

Academic Enhancement Center The Academic Enhancement Center (“AEC”) supports student learning and academic success through scaffolding student engagement with course content, helpi ng with the development of metacognitive strategies and skills, critical thinking, writing, time management, and test taking skills.
AEC programs are primarily peer-to-peer, enabling the Center to support the development of collaborative learning skills fo r all students, as well as teaching and leadership skills for student staff.

The AEC offers unique resources including three forms of tutoring in the STEM disciplines; an Academic Skills Development programming, including UCS 160; and the Writing Center for helping students at all levels of writing skills development.
The mission of the Academic Enhancement Center is to help students invest in their academic success.
The AEC learning support programs and services empower students to become more skillful and successful.
The AEC is committed to responding to student needs, collaborating with faculty and providing professional development for the student staff with the goal of enhancing student learning.
Feinstein Scholars Income from an endowment provides support for undergraduates in the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and other academic programs.
These scholarships are targeted to Rhode Island students who were Feinstein Junior Scholars.
Pell Summer Promise Program In an effort to support Pell students in completing their education in a timely manner , URI launched the Pell Summer Promise Program uses Federal Pell support and URI aid to help our most needy in- State students take free summer courses.

The goal is to enhance their time to degree and make college more affordable.
COMMUNITY, EQUITY AND DIVERSITY The Office of Community, Equity and Diversity leads institution- wide initiatives to anchor inclusion in every aspect of the University of Rhode Island’s community and operations.
The Office strives to advance inclusive excellence through impacting culture and climate by creating a welcoming community where each member can learn, work, and thrive; hosting communities of practice that foster cultural competence and model constructive dialogue a cross difference; incentivizing inclusivity in scholarship, research, pedagogy, and practices; incorporating inclusion in University policies and procedures by identifying and removing artificial barriers that impede the land grant mission and mandate to s upport all learners; and, iterating through coordinated and ongoing institution-wide assessment.

In addition, the Office of Community, Equity and Diversity oversees four centers that promote diversity, equity and inclusion: Women’s Center The URI Women’s Center partners with others in the URI community to provide an empowering space which promotes social justice for every member of the community, regardless of gender, gender identity, body, ability, sexual orientation, race, spirituality, and ethnicity.
C ommunity members are encouraged to

A-23 engage and foster continual dialogue on gender and issues that disproportionately affect woman-identified persons and their allies.
By developing, supporting and advocating for woman-identified persons’ abilities, talents, values and diverse identities, the URI Women’s Center supports all University students, faculty and staff in expanding their positive potential, agency and life experience.
Multicultural Student Services Center The URI Multicultural Student Services Center is dedicated to developing a supportive and inclusive campus culture across the boundaries of culture, identity, and discipline.
Celebrating unity in diversity, the Multicultural Center invites all students, fa culty, staff, administrators, alumni, and other friends to join in its work in creating a community of learners within and beyond URI.
The URI Multicultural Center collaboratively provides programs and resources that engage, connect and support the URI com munity in becoming just and culturally competent global citizens.
It also houses The Center for Nonviolence and Peace which promotes and studies approaches to addressing conflict through nonviolence.

Gender and Sexuality Center The URI Gender and Sexuali ty Center encourages students, faculty, and staff to explore and affirm their multiple and intersecting identities, especially surrounding gender and sexuality.
Through education, advocacy, and community- building, the Gender and Sexuality Center strives to cultivate an inclusive campus culture that celebrates all genders and sexual identities.
The Center provides intersectional programming and collaborates with student leaders and campus partners to strengthen community and foster belonging, all while nurtu ring a student-centered environment that supports academic and personal growth.
Center for Military and Veteran Education The Center for Military and Veteran Education serves and supports prior, present, and future military - connected students, faculty, an d staff as they further their educational and professional objectives.
The Center assists in the transition from military life into student life and beyond and helps veterans connect with the resources and networks of support available to them at URI and within the local community.

STUDENT SERVICES Auxiliary Services Auxiliary services consist of housing, dining, student union, health center and the campus store, which depend on restricted fees and related revenues derived from student clients.
These operations are required by State law to be fully self-supporting.
Undergraduate Housing On-campus residence halls are available to eligible students during the regular academic year and winter inter-session, with additional availability offered provided during the summer.
The University offers a variety of living accommodations with 27 residence halls and two apartment complexes.
The residence halls include 22 traditional residence halls, of which fourteen primarily house first year resident Living and Learning Communities, and three undergraduate apartment -style facilities, including the new Brookside apartment-style residence hall completed in January 2020.
There are also two International Engineering Program Houses.
First year students are strongly encouraged to live on campus other than in exceptional circumstances; in the fall of 2024 approximately 88% of URI first year students live in residence halls.

In the fall 202 4 semester, 579 University students reside in the fraternity/sorority system which sponsors 16 sororities and fraternities (the “Greek” houses) located on university land but not owned or operated by the University.

The Greek houses

Graduate Housing On-campus apartments are available primarily for graduate students.

Counseling Services.
The Counseling Center is staffed by licensed mental health counselors, psychologists, and social workers.
The Center offers indi vidual counseling and a variety of skill -building and support groups to help undergraduate and graduate students achieve their academic and life goals.

The Counseling Center provides assistance to students in areas such as adjusting to college life, coping with stress, building satisfying relationships, planning for the future, and coping with anxiety depression, substance use, or other mental health challenges.
The University partners with Telus Health to provide free, confidential, emotional health and wellbeing support, including access to clinicians 24/7 virtually, by phone or chat.
University Chaplains.
The University chaplains are active in providing religious services and in counseling, advising campus gro ups, teaching, and programming.

Memorial Union.
The center for campus programs and activities, the Memorial Union houses a wide variety of education, social and cultural services and facilities for undergraduate and graduate students.

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES The University’s Information Technology Services organization (“ITS”) provides leadership and strategic direction for technology and ente rprise systems that support the University of Rhode Island community.

ITS supports key systems used every day, including the Learning Management System for online classes, Enterprise Resource Planning systems for student records, HR, and finances, and the Help Desk, which provides technical support to the entire URI community.
ITS also manages the University's high -speed internet network, which links URI’s campuses to each other and to the wider world through a secure, multi- gigabit fiber-optic connection.
With growing demand for advanced technology in classrooms and research, ITS is strengthening its support for artificial intelligence, machine learning, and high -performance computing.
These advancements position URI as a leader in research and discovery.
F aculty and students use AI to create predictive healthcare models, develop early disease detection tools, and analyze large datasets to support public health and environmental sustainability.
High-performance computing drives major research in climate modeling, fisheries science, and coastal resilience, which are critical to Rhode Island’s future.
Enhanced computational resources enable faster simulations, large-scale data analysis, and breakthroughs in complex scientific challenges.

These tools increase UR I’s competitiveness for research grants from agencies like the National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health.
They support faculty -driven research on national priorities and provide students with experience in cutting- edge technologies.
Students trained in AI and high - performance computing are well -positioned for careers in data science, engineering, and emerging technology fields.
Cybersecurity is a growing challenge for all institutions, and URI is no exception.
To protect sensitive information, ITS has strengthened its security systems.
This includes requiring multi-factor authentication

A-26 for most University systems, upgrading network security to prevent unauthorized access, and rebuilding URI's disaster recovery system to protect against ransomware attacks.
By supporting student learning, research, and day-to-day operations, ITS ensures that URI stays connected, secure, and ready for the future.
Strategic investments in areas like online learning, campus Wi-Fi, research tools, and cybersecurity help ensure that students and faculty have the resources they need to succeed.

Higgins Welcome Center.

The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering (College of Engineering Phase I).

On October 7, 2019, the University dedicated The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering, a new 187,000 square foot building.

Meade Stadium Artificial Turf.

Water Filtration Plant.

At the end of the Fiscal Year 2022 legislative session, the Rhode Island General Assembly enacted legislation that establishes a concentration limit of 20 parts per trillion of Per - and Polyfluorinated Substances (“PFAS”) in public drinking water supplies.
The legislation initially required full compliance no later than July 1, 2023 but was amended on July 1, 2023 that extended compliance requirements.
The legislation established the Rhode Island Department of Health as the regulatory body for monitoring compliance with this new standard.
The Environmental Protection Agency in March 2023 has similarly proposed to establish legally enforceable levels for six PFAS known to occur in drinking water, and this proposed rule is currently out for comment.
The University, which is licensed as a municipal-level water system subject to the newly enacted Rhode Island law, received $20 million in RICAP funds support from the state of Rhode Island to design and construct a water system filtration plant.
As of November 2024, the first phase of construction of the filtration plant was completed with that phase 1 effort successfully supplying “PFAS-free” water to the campus.

Next steps include completing design efforts for Phase 2 of the filtration plant that expands the plants capabilities and extends the useful life of the plant for the next 20-30 years.
The university is working with the RI State Purchases office to implement a “design/ build/ operate” contract that is anticipated to be awarded in the late summer of 2025, with intended phase 2 completion by December 2026.

ENTERPRISE RISK MANAGEMENT The University has instituted an Enterprise Risk Management (“ERM”) program.
ERM is the formal and systematic effort to control the impact of uncertainty and variability on an organization’s strategic objectives by managing risks at all levels of the organization.
ERM differs from traditional risk management by taking a holistic approach to managing risk.
The ERM program promotes a culture of compliance and shared responsibility at URI.
It manages and protect the human, physical, natural, and financial assets of the University community, and aim to minimize losses and legal liabilities.
The program provides technical expertise, educational programs, support, and consultation to the University community to achieve a culture of risk management.
As part of the ERM prog ram, the University procures appropriate insurance as one of many risk control and mitigation measures.

The University is insured for various risks of loss arising out of claims for negligence, including bodily injury and property damage, wrongful acts, cy ber liability, professional liability and workers compensation through a combination of insurance policies and self -insurance.
The University participates in the State’s property insurance program, which covers University buildings and contents against risks of direct physical loss, on a blanket, replacement cost basis.
Total property value for the University’s four campuses is currently reported as $ 2.3 billion and insured to the extent that losses exceed $200,000 per incident, or per building if the loss is due to a named storm, and do not exceed $240 million per occurrence.
Within ERM, the Office of Equal Opportunity assists the university in creating and maintaining a learning and working environment free from discrimination and harassment through the administration of the University’s civil rights compliance programs.
ERM also administers the University’s Title IX program.
PUBLIC SAFETY Fostering a safe and secure environment for those who live, learn, work and visit is paramount at the University.

The Department of Public Safety supports the University with a sworn police department, office of emergency management, emergency dispatch and communications, fire and life safety, alarm services, transportation and parking services, and administration division.
The URI Police Department is responsible for and has jurisdiction over all URI campuses and is staffed by sworn University Police Officers and non- sworn campus patrol persons.
The department patrols on the

A-30 Kingston campus 24/7 and respond to calls for service at all satellite campuses including the Narragansett Bay Campus and Rhode Island Nursing Education Center (RINEC) in Providence.
The Office of Emergency Management provides planning and services for preparedness, response, recovery, prevention and mitigation and serves as the liaison with other local, state, and federal emergency providers and responders.
Transportation and Parking provides safe, sustainable, reliable, and cost -effective transportation and parking services that facilitate convenient access to the University by students, faculty, staff, and visitors.
Our key services include providing campus transportation shuttles, utilizing patrols and technology to enforce parking regulations, and promoting more sustainable transportation options.
Transportation and Parking operates a comprehensive shuttle system managed by the University using a private vendor.
The service is widely used by students living both on and off -campus, as well as faculty and staff.
In addition, the Rhody Safe Rides service provides late- night on- demand rides to enhance student security.

The Transportation and Parking Office uses technology which streamlines the purchase of parking permits for a better customer experience and increased efficiency.
Throughout the year, new and returning students and all community members receive print, web, video and email information and training about resources available to protect them against injury, fire and other threats and to ensure that the University continues its mission in a safe, secure, and inclusive environment.
URI Public Safety takes a community policing approach to their work, and the URI Police are an integral part of the daily life of the University.

Parlange, Ph.D., P.Eng., President DATE: June 26, 2025 SUBJECT: Action Item: Approval of the Certain Documents Relative to the Development, Construction, and Financing of New University Housing Purpose of Submittal: To recommend the Board of Trustees Finance and Facilities Committee recommend approval to the Board of Trustees of the New University Housing (NUH) Project and authorize execution of documents for the development, construction, and financing of two new on- campus undergraduate student housing communities and one graduate student and family housing community at the University of Rhode Island.
Background: In late 2022, the University of Rhode Island engaged a planning team led by Scion Advisory Services, with architects from CannonDesign, to develop a Housing and Residential Life Housing Master Plan to transform URI housing.

This initiative align ed with URI’s strategic commitment to enhanc e the student experience by providing modern, affordable, and desirable living spaces.
The plan recommended that URI pursue a public-private-partnership (P3) to address immediate housing needs on the Kingston campus.
In May 2024, URI issued a public request for proposal for a development partner, and after a thorough vetting process, selected Gilbane Development Company (Gilbane) as its P3 partner.
In September 2024, the University entered into a Preliminary Development Agreement (PDA) with Gilbane.
In March 2025, the University approved the feasibility study conducted by Gilbane confirming that the project was feasible and would move forward.
Gilbane then selected, with URI’s concurrence, Provident to serve as the project 501(c)(3) partner.
PRG – RI Properties LLC, a single member limited liability company, was organized by Provident for the Project.
URI DevCo LLC, a single purpose subsidiary of Gilbane, was also organized for development of the Project.

In April 2025, URI DevCo, Provident, and Raymond James (underwriter) commenced the application process to issue debt through the Rhode Island Health and Education Building Corporation (RIHEBC).
The Project is summarized below.
Project Overview: Project Scope & Design: • Total Beds: 1,134 • Planned Housing Phases: o Occupancy in Fall 2027: 514 undergraduate beds o Occupancy in Fall 2028: 400 undergraduate beds o Occupancy in Fall 2028: 220 graduate beds

• Building Types: o Undergraduate Housing (Two Buildings): Apartment-style, single bedrooms in two- and four- bedroom units.
Modular construction. o Graduate Housing (Six Buildings + Community Center): Apartments with studio, one-bedroom, two-bedroom, and three-bedroom configurations.
Modular rebuild on existing foundations. o All buildings meet state code and URI design standards.
Financial Summary (rounded): • Total Project Cost: $231MM (as of June 2025). • URI Equity Contribution: The University may fund an equity contribution to the Project, the amount of which is currently subject to negotiation, and will be up to the amount authorized by the Board during executive session. • Rental Rates: Rental rates are within acceptable range to URI Housing and Residential Life, though may need to increase due to changes in market conditions. • Annual Rate Escalation: 3% • Expected Occupancy Rate: 95% • Debt Term: 40 years (all-in). • Debt Coverage Ratio: 1.2x or better (Senior Debt). • Residual Cash Flow to URI: $317MM over the term (NPV @ 5% = $63.7MM).

Document Approval Over the past several months, the University has negotiated and vetted several Project documents, three of which are being brought to the Board today for approval, and two of which are being shared for informational purposes.

These documents, listed below, are described in more detail in the enclosed Board of Trustees resolutions. • The Ground Lease between the University and the Provident , will extend for a term of up to 42 years and will contain provisions requiring the Project to be constructed in accordance with campus standards (for approval). • The Affiliation Agreement between the University and Provident , which outlines each entity’s obligations to the project (for approval). • The Interim Management Agreement between the University and URI DevCo LLC, which will allow the University to continue to manage the graduate student housing until the expected turnover date of May 2026, at which time it will be turned over to the Developer for demolition and re -construction (for approval). • The Turnkey Development Agreement between URI DevCo LLC and Provident, pursuant to which the Developer will implement the design, construction, and commissioning of the Project for a stipulated sum in accordance with plans approved by the University (for information). • The Project Management Agreement between Provident and Inwood Management, outlining operations and maintenance of the Student Housing Facilities (for information).

Next Steps Upon the Board’s approval of the Project and authorization to continue negotiating required documents, URI will finalize the negotiation and execute the relevant documents.
The Project is scheduled for financial close in September 2025, at which point the final Project budget will be determined.
We look forward to continued collaboration with Gilbane to ensure this critical project’s seamless and successful implementation.

Public-Private Partnership Project Summary and Scope The Project is structured as a concession agreement with a private qualified development firm to enter into a public -private partnership (“ P3”), which requires a ground lease for the structure and the issuance of bonds by the Rhode Island Health and Educational Building Corporation (the “ Issuer”).
This P3 is a delivery approach , whereby, w hen appropriate and feasible, the University can utilize the P3 model to secure the anticipated advantages of increased speed of delivery, guaranteed maximum price and fi rm delivery date, and sharing risk with the private sector.
In a P3 model, the University leases its land to a tax-exempt nonprofit entity in the form of a ground lease.
That entity engages the developer and contractors to construct the buildings.
The nonprofit entity owns the buildings until the debt is retired.
At that time, ownership reverts to the University, and the ground lease terminates.
Development Process In support of this Project planning, the University solicited proposals on April 30, 2024 for the development and construction of the Student Housing Facilities.

As a result of the solicitation process, Gilbane Development Company, a Rhode Island corporation , was chosen as the lead developer to implement the development financing, construction, equipping, and operation of the

3 4900-8991-3674.4 Project.
URI DevCo LLC, a single purpose subsidiary of Gilbane Development Company , was organized by Gilbane Development Company for development of the Project (the “Developer”).
As a part of the team, Provident Resources Group, Inc ., a nonprofit 501(c)(3) tax -exempt organization established to assist colleges and universities across the country in providing academic and related facilities for their students and otherwise furthering their education missions, (“Provident”) will serve as the tax-exempt parent and sole member of the ground lessee and owner of the facilities , PRG – RI Properties LLC, a single member limited liability company (the “Lessee/Borrower”).
The Lessee/Borrower will be organized exclusively to carry out the Project and is not expected to have any assets other than those that are associated with the Project .
The selected team includes Gilbane Building Company, a Rhode Island corporation, as the general contractor and Raymond James as the underwriter .
The architecture partner is CannonDesign.
Inwood Management will perform operations and maintenance of the Student Housing Facilities.

Following the award to the Developer, the University for itself and on behalf of the Board entered into a pre liminary development agreement with the Developer to conduct pre -development and design activities for the Project as a whole before bond issuance and closing, currently targeted for September 1, 2025, which date may be subject to change.
The entire process that led to the award of this transaction was reviewed and approved by the Rhode Island Division of Purchases through the URI Office of Strategic Procurement.
Project Structure, Financing and Document Package The total cost of the Project is currently estimated to be approximately $231M, which is expected to be financed through the bond issuance by the Issuer.
The proceeds of the bonds will be l oaned by the Issuer to the Lessee/Borrower.
The University may also fund an equity contribution, the amount of which is currently subject to negotiation and will be up to the amount authorized by the Board during executive session.
The proposed financing structure for the Project will be based on a privatized P3 financi ng model through which the Board will ground lease the land on which the Project is located to the Lessee/Borrower.

The Ground Lease for the Project between the University and the Lessee/Borrower (the “Ground Lease”) will extend for a term of up to 42 years, which will be in excess of the maturity of the proposed bond financing, and will contain provisions requiring the Project to be constructed in accordance with campus standards.
Provisions in the Ground Lease and Affiliation Agreement will also include certain areas of support and cooperation between the University and the Lessee/Borrower.
Under the Ground Lease, the land will always remain owned by the University, and the Lessee/Borrower will own the Student Housing Facilities for the term of the financing.
Annual rent to the University will be Net Available Cash Flow from the Project, estimated over the life of the lease to be approximately $317,157,460.
A copy of the form of the Ground Lease, subject to further negotiation and execution as described herein, is attached hereto.

The University and the Lessee/Borrower will also enter into an affiliation agreement (“Affiliation Agreement”) to provide for the University’s obligations with respect to the Project, including the leasing of the Undergraduate Housing Project consistent with its leasing of other on- campus undergraduate student housing.
A copy of the form of the Affiliation Agreement, subject to further negotiation and execution as described herein, is attached hereto.

4 4900-8991-3674.4 The Graduate Student Housing Facility will be turned over to the Developer for demolition and reconstruction after the end of the 2025 -2026 academic year.
During the period between closing and turnover, the University will continue to manage the existing graduate village housing consistent with existing management practices pursuant to an interim management agreement (the “Interim Management Agreement”).
A copy of the form of Interim Management Agreement , subject to further negotiation and execution as described herein, is attached hereto.
The Developer and the Lessee/Borrower will enter into a turnkey development agreement (the “Turnkey Development Agreement”) pursuant to which the Developer will implement the design, construction, and commissioning of the Project for a stipulated sum in accordance with plans approved by the University.
The Turnkey Development Agreement is expected to be in substantially the form attached hereto.

Pursuant to the Management Agreement between Lessee/Borrower and Inwood Management (the “Management Agreement”), Inwood Management will perform operations and maintenance of the Student Housing Facilities , including all leasing and management of the Graduate Student Housing Facility, in accordance with the Responsibility Matrix attached to the Management Agreement.
The Management Agreement is expected to be in substantially the form attached hereto.
P3 Agreement Package The University, for itself and on behalf of the Board of Trustees, is required to enter into a series of agreements with the Lessee/Borrower and Developer to authorize and complete the Project, and to give such approvals and take such other actions and enter into other agreements consistent with the Ground Lease, as the parties consider necessary and appropriate in connection with the development, construction, financing, and operation of the Project as described above .

The principal documents that the Authorized Officer will execute will be the Ground Lease, the Affiliation Agreement and the Interim Management Agreement, each substantially in the form of the listed agreements attached hereto, subject to such further negotiation and changes as any Authorized Officer executing any such document may approve .
URI has also been actively engaged in the review and negotiation of the Turnkey Develo pment Agreement and Property Management Agreement to ensure they align with the University’s overarching goals and desired outcomes of the Project.
